blocks.name: Anatomy
blocks.def: The study of body structures and the relationships among them. The word derives from the Greek anatome (ana- "up," tome- "a cutting"), meaning "a cutting up" — i.e. dissection.

blocks.x: Anatomy is distinct from (but closely tied to) physiology, which studies how those structures function.
Branches of Anatomy

blocks.name: Gross (macroscopic) anatomy
blocks.def: Study of structures visible to the naked eye; includes regional, systemic, and surface anatomy.

blocks.name: Microscopic anatomy (histology)
blocks.def: Study of structures too small to see unaided; subdivided into cytology (study of cells) and histology (study of tissues).

blocks.name: Developmental anatomy
blocks.def: Study of structural changes across the lifespan; embryology specifically covers developmental changes occurring before birth.

blocks.name: Surface (topographical) anatomy
blocks.def: Study of surface markings of the body to understand internal anatomy through visualization and palpation.

blocks.name: Radiographic anatomy
blocks.def: Study of internal body structures using imaging techniques (X-ray, MRI, CT, etc.).

items: 275 BC, Alexandria — Herophilus conducts early systematic anatomical study.
600–1100 — Knowledge of Greek anatomy transferred to Western Europe; Islamic scholars translate Greek anatomical treatises into Arabic.
1100s–1500s — Galen's works translated from Arabic into Latin, and later directly from the Greek originals.
1235 — The first European medical school is founded at Salerno, Italy; human bodies are publicly dissected.
1490 — An anatomical theatre opens in Padua, Italy.
1491 — The first illustrated printed medical book is published in Venice: Johannes de Ketham's Fasciculus medicinae.
1600–1900 — Anatomy plays a central role in medical education and research.

blocks.x: Anatomy has its own vocabulary — anatomical nomenclature — largely built from Greek and Latin word parts, plus eponyms (terms named after people, e.g. Adam's apple, Eustachian tube, Sertoli cells, Achilles <term d="A strong cord of fibrous tissue that attaches muscle to bone.">tendon</term>).
Medical terms are built from up to four word parts, combined to give a specific meaning:

blocks.name: Word root
blocks.def: The foundation/core of a medical word, conveying its fundamental meaning. Every medical term contains at least one. Example: in HEPAT/ITIS, "HEPAT" (liver) is the word root.

blocks.name: Prefix
blocks.def: Attached to the beginning of a word root to influence its meaning. Not every term has one. Example: in SUB/HEPAT/IC, "SUB-" (under) is the prefix — subhepatic means "pertaining to under the liver."

blocks.name: Suffix
blocks.def: Attached to the end of a word root to alter or modify its meaning. Example: in HEPAT/ITIS, "-ITIS" (inflammation) is the suffix.

blocks.x: Common Prefixes

blocks.name: Epi-
blocks.def: Upon/over. Example: epicardium (over the heart).

blocks.name: En-/Endo-
blocks.def: Within. Example: endocardium.

blocks.name: Gastro-
blocks.def: Stomach. Example: gastritis.

blocks.name: Infra-
blocks.def: Below. Example: infraorbital.

blocks.name: Myo-
blocks.def: Muscle. Example: myometrium.

blocks.name: Retro-
blocks.def: Behind. Example: retroperitoneal.

blocks.name: A-/An-
blocks.def: No/without. Example: anaemia, aphasia.

blocks.name: Ante-
blocks.def: Before. Example: antepartum.

blocks.name: Anti-
blocks.def: Against. Example: antibiotic.

blocks.name: Dys-
blocks.def: Difficult. Example: dysphagia.

blocks.name: Hemi-
blocks.def: Half. Example: hemiplegia.

blocks.name: Hyper-
blocks.def: Above/excessive. Example: hyperglycemia.

blocks.name: Hypo-
blocks.def: Below/deficient. Example: hypodermic.

blocks.name: Inter-
blocks.def: Between. Example: intercostal.

blocks.name: Intra-
blocks.def: Within. Example: intracranial.

blocks.name: Peri-
blocks.def: Around. Example: peritoneum.

blocks.name: Poly-
blocks.def: Many. Example: polyarthritis.

blocks.name: Post-
blocks.def: After. Example: postoperative.

blocks.name: Pro-
blocks.def: Before. Example: prophylaxis.

blocks.name: Trans-
blocks.def: Across. Example: transabdominal.

blocks.x: Common Suffixes

blocks.name: -algia / -odynia
blocks.def: Pain. Examples: neuralgia, gastrodynia.

blocks.name: -ectomy
blocks.def: Cutting out (surgical removal). Example: hepatectomy.

blocks.name: -itis
blocks.def: Inflammation.

blocks.name: -ology
blocks.def: Study of.

blocks.name: -pathy
blocks.def: Suffering from / disease of. Example: neuropathy.

blocks.name: -scopy / -scope
blocks.def: To view / a visual exam instrument. Example: bronchoscope.

blocks.name: -otomy / -stomy
blocks.def: Surgical opening.

blocks.name: -emia
blocks.def: Blood condition. Examples: anaemia, leukaemia.

blocks.name: -oma
blocks.def: Tumour (benign or malignant). Examples: lymphoma, sarcoma.

blocks.name: -plasty
blocks.def: Surgical repair. Example: rhinoplasty.

blocks.name: -rrhagia / -rrhage
blocks.def: Severe bleeding. Example: hemorrhage.

blocks.name: -spasm
blocks.def: Contraction. Example: bronchospasm.

blocks.name: -stenosis
blocks.def: Tightening/narrowing. Example: aortostenosis.

blocks.x: Combining Forms

blocks.name: Arthro-
blocks.def: Joint. Examples: arthritis, arthroscopy.

blocks.name: Carcin/o-
blocks.def: Cancer. Example: carcinoma.

blocks.name: Cyst/o-
blocks.def: Fluid-filled. Example: cystitis.

blocks.name: Cyto-
blocks.def: Cell. Example: cytology.

blocks.name: Erythro-
blocks.def: Red. Example: erythrocytosis.

blocks.name: Thrombo-
blocks.def: Clot. Example: thrombosis.

blocks.name: Viscera
blocks.def: Internal organ. Example: visceral.

blocks.x: Plural Forms

items: words ending "-a" → "-e": vertebra → vertebrae, bursa → bursae
words ending "-us" → "-i": alveolus → alveoli, uterus → uteri, malleolus → malleoli

blocks.name: Anatomical position
blocks.def: The standard reference position: standing upright, head/eyes/toes directed forward, arms adjacent to the sides with palms facing forward, lower limbs together with feet parallel and toes forward.

blocks.cap: The anatomical position — the standard reference posture used throughout anatomical description.

blocks.x: All directional and positional terms in anatomy are defined relative to this standard position, regardless of the body's actual orientation (lying down, etc.).
Anatomical Planes

blocks.name: Median plane
blocks.def: A vertical plane running longitudinally through the body, dividing it into left and right halves.

blocks.name: <term d="A vertical cut running front to back that divides the body into left and right parts.">Sagittal plane</term>
blocks.def: Any vertical plane parallel to the median plane. A "parasagittal" plane is any sagittal plane except the median one.

blocks.name: Coronal (frontal) plane
blocks.def: A vertical plane at 90° to the median plane, dividing the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior).

blocks.name: Transverse (horizontal) plane
blocks.def: A horizontal plane dividing the body into upper and lower segments.

blocks.cap: The three main anatomical planes: sagittal, coronal, and transverse.
Anatomical planes shown relative to the standard anatomical position.

blocks.x: These paired terms describe the position of one structure relative to another, always assuming the anatomical position:

blocks.name: <term d="Closer to the surface of the body.">Superficial</term> / Intermediate / Deep
blocks.def: Closer to vs. further from the body surface.

blocks.name: <term d="Nearer to the trunk or to the point where a limb attaches.">Proximal</term> / <term d="Further away from the trunk or from the point where a limb attaches.">Distal</term>
blocks.def: Closer to vs. further from the point of attachment/origin (mainly used for limbs).

blocks.name: Medial / Lateral
blocks.def: Closer to vs. further from the median plane (midline).

blocks.name: Posterior (dorsal) / Anterior (ventral)
blocks.def: Toward the back vs. toward the front.

blocks.name: Inferior (caudal) / Superior (cranial)
blocks.def: Toward the feet vs. toward the head.

blocks.name: Bilateral / Unilateral
blocks.def: Occurring on both sides vs. one side of the body.

blocks.name: Ipsilateral / Contralateral
blocks.def: On the same side vs. the opposite side (relative to a reference structure).

blocks.cap: Terms of relationship, comparison, and laterality shown on the body.

blocks.x: Anatomical movement terms describe how a joint or body part moves relative to the anatomical position.

blocks.name: <term d="A movement that decreases the angle at a joint, bending it.">Flexion</term>
blocks.def: Bending a joint, or decreasing the angle between two bones. In the fetal position, the joints are flexed.

blocks.name: <term d="A movement that increases the angle at a joint, straightening it.">Extension</term>
blocks.def: Straightening a joint, or increasing the angle between two bones. In the anatomical position, the joints are extended.

blocks.name: Hyperextension
blocks.def: Excessive extension of a joint beyond the anatomical position.

blocks.name: <term d="Movement of a body part away from the midline of the body.">Abduction</term>
blocks.def: Moving a body part away from the midline of the body.

blocks.name: <term d="Movement of a body part back toward the midline of the body.">Adduction</term>
blocks.def: Moving a body part toward the midline of the body.

blocks.name: <term d="Rotating the forearm so the palm faces downward or backward.">Pronation</term>
blocks.def: Turning the arm or foot downward (palm or sole facing down); the resulting position is "prone."

blocks.name: <term d="Rotating the forearm so the palm faces upward or forward.">Supination</term>
blocks.def: Turning the arm or foot upward (palm or sole facing up); the resulting position is "supine."

blocks.name: Inversion
blocks.def: Turning the sole of the foot inward.

blocks.name: Eversion
blocks.def: Turning the sole of the foot outward.

blocks.name: Dorsiflexion
blocks.def: Ankle movement bringing the foot upward, toward the shin.

blocks.name: Plantarflexion
blocks.def: Ankle movement pointing the foot downward.

blocks.name: Retraction
blocks.def: Moving a body part backward.

blocks.name: Protraction
blocks.def: Moving a body part forward.

blocks.name: Elevation
blocks.def: Raising a body part.

blocks.name: Depression
blocks.def: Lowering a body part.

blocks.name: Rotation
blocks.def: Turning a body part on a single axis.

blocks.name: <term d="A circular movement combining flexion, extension, abduction and adduction.">Circumduction</term>
blocks.def: A tri-planar, circular motion, seen at multiaxial joints like the hip or shoulder.

blocks.name: Internal (medial) rotation
blocks.def: Rotation of the hip or shoulder toward the midline.

blocks.name: External (lateral) rotation
blocks.def: Rotation of the hip or shoulder away from the midline.

blocks.name: Radial deviation
blocks.def: Movement of the wrist toward the radius (lateral side).

blocks.name: Ulnar deviation
blocks.def: Movement of the wrist toward the ulna (medial side).

blocks.name: Opposition
blocks.def: Movement of the thumb across the palm of the hand, to touch the other digits.

items: Lithotomy position — lying on the back with hips and knees flexed, thighs apart and supported (used in certain examinations/procedures).

blocks.x: The body is divided into major regions for descriptive purposes: head, neck, thorax, abdomen, pelvis/perineum, upper limb, lower limb, and back.
Body Cavities

blocks.name: Dorsal body cavity
blocks.def: Lined by three membrane layers called meninges. Contains the cranial cavity (houses the brain) and the spinal/vertebral cavity (houses the spinal cord).

blocks.name: Ventral body cavity
blocks.def: Lined by serous membrane. Subdivided into the pericardial cavity (lined by pericardium, contains the heart), the pleural cavities (lined by pleurae, contain the lungs), and the abdominopelvic cavity (abdominal + pelvic cavities, lined by peritoneum; contains the digestive organs, spleen, kidneys, rectum, bladder, and reproductive organs).

blocks.cap: The major body cavities: dorsal (cranial + spinal) and ventral (thoracic + abdominopelvic).

blocks.name: Parietal pleura
blocks.def: Lines the wall of the thoracic cavity.

blocks.name: Visceral pleura
blocks.def: Covers the surface of the lung itself; together with the parietal pleura, encloses the pleural cavity.

blocks.x: Abdominal Regions

Four abdominal quadrants and nine abdominal regions are clinically important for describing the position of a mass, localizing a patient's pain, or the location of abdominal viscera. The quadrants are formed by the median and transumbilical planes; the 9 regions are formed by two midclavicular planes plus the subcostal (transpyloric) and transtubercular planes.

blocks.name: Abdominal quadrants
blocks.def: Four regions — right upper, left upper, right lower, and left lower quadrant — formed by the median and transumbilical planes.

blocks.name: The 9 abdominal regions
blocks.def: Right hypochondrium, epigastrium, left hypochondrium, right lumbar (lateral), umbilical, left lumbar (lateral), right inguinal (groin), hypogastrium, and left inguinal (groin). Clinically, tenderness in the right iliac fossa/right inguinal region is a classic sign of appendicitis.

blocks.name: Integumentary system
blocks.def: Skin, nails, hair, and cutaneous glands. Functions: protection, containment of body structures, water retention, vitamin D synthesis, thermoregulation, and cutaneous sensation.

blocks.x: Naming Skeletal Muscles

blocks.name: Agonist (prime mover)
blocks.def: The muscle primarily responsible for producing a particular movement.

blocks.name: Antagonist
blocks.def: A muscle that opposes or reverses the action of the agonist.

blocks.name: Synergist
blocks.def: A muscle that assists the agonist, either by contributing to the same movement or by reducing unwanted/unnecessary movement.

blocks.name: Fixator
blocks.def: A specialized synergist that immobilizes the origin of a prime mover so that all contractile tension is exerted at its insertion — important for maintaining posture.

blocks.x: Muscles are often named for the bone they're associated with (e.g. the temporalis overlies the temporal bone), for their number of origins (biceps = two, triceps = three, quadriceps = four), for the direction of their fibers relative to the midline (rectus = straight, as in rectus abdominis; transversus = transverse; obliquus = obliquely inclined), or for their relative size (maximus = largest, minimus = smallest, longus = long, brevis = short — e.g. gluteus maximus vs. gluteus minimus).

blocks.name: Fascicle arrangement
blocks.def: The pattern in which a muscle's fascicles (bundles of muscle fibers) are arranged, which determines the muscle's structure and force/range-of-motion characteristics. The most common patterns are circular, convergent, parallel, and pennate.

blocks.x: Radiological anatomy studies body structure and function using medical imaging techniques — the use of different imaging modalities to visualize anatomic structures for diagnosis and treatment. Common methods include:

items: Nuclear medicine scans — PET, SPECT, bone scans, sentinel lymph node mapping.

blocks.name: Plain X-ray (radiograph)
blocks.def: An electromagnetic wave of very short wavelength (classed as a carcinogen). Best for visualizing bones and abnormally dense structures. High-density tissue (bone) absorbs more X-rays and appears white; low-density tissue (lungs) absorbs fewer and appears dark.

blocks.name: Bone densitometry (DEXA scan)
blocks.def: Uses X-rays (or CT) to measure bone mineral density, especially calcium — used to diagnose osteoporosis ("porous bone").

blocks.name: Fluoroscopy
blocks.def: Uses X-rays in real time to create moving images of the body.

blocks.x: Contrast agents (such as barium or iodine salts) can be used with conventional radiography to visualize luminal or vascular structures — like the digestive tract — that wouldn't otherwise show up on a plain X-ray.
PA vs. AP Chest X-Ray

blocks.name: PA (Posteroanterior) chest X-ray
blocks.def: The most frequently requested imaging test; gives a good assessment of cardiac size and avoids magnifying the heart, since the film sits close to the anterior chest wall. Scapulae lie in the periphery; clavicles project over the lung fields.

blocks.name: AP (Anteroposterior) chest X-ray
blocks.def: Used when a patient can't achieve a normal PA position (e.g. bedbound patients); common in intensive care for diagnosing acute and chronic conditions.
